clue.text: Joe knew Sam vaguely in Simon play

indicators.note: done vaguely, the letters of the three names lose their order and are rearranged

explanation.surface: Three men with ordinary names drift through a play by Neil Simon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vaguely' signals an anagram of JOEKNEWSAM. Neil Simon's comedy is about a novelist and the women in his life.
explanation.definitionFit: Jake's Women is a 1992 comedy by the American playwright Neil Simon.

clue.text: Slow movement of present era conversion charge

parts.note: AD (anno Domini) marks the present era of dates
agio is the fee charged for changing one currency into another

explanation.surface: A banker grumbles at the fee for changing money in modern times.
explanation.definitionFit: In music, an adagio is a slow movement of a larger piece.

clue.text: For example, the French love of Shakespearian knight

parts.note: EG is short for exempli gratia, for example
le, the French for 'the', shortens to L' before a vowel
amour is the French word for love

explanation.surface: A French romance of the kind a Shakespearean knight might sigh over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the French' gives L', the French article as it stands before a vowel.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Eglamour is a knight who helps Silvia escape in The Two Gentlemen of Verona.

clue.text: Evelina's Sir Clement less of a disappointment than Marianne Dashwood's John

explanation.surface: Comparing two literary cads to see which let the heroine down less.
explanation.walkthrough: Fanny Burney's Evelina is pestered by Sir Clement Willoughby; in Austen's Sense and Sensibility Marianne Dashwood is jilted by John Willoughby. 'less of a disappointment than' is linking commentary.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are rakish suitors sharing one surname, one in Burney's novel and one in Austen's.

clue.text: Merry, reckless folk like Berowne, Maria thought

explanation.surface: A character in a comedy is judged by a lady to be a wild joker.
explanation.walkthrough: In Love's Labour's Lost Maria calls Berowne a 'merry mad-cap lord'.
explanation.definitionFit: Impulsive pranksters are wild jesters; Maria's phrase in Love's Labour's Lost puts Berowne among them.

clue.text: "And carried half-way home or Pints and quarts" (Housman

definitions.text: "And carried half-way home or Pints and quarts" (Housman

parts.words: "And carried half-way home or Pints and quarts" (Housman
parts.note: a quotation from A Shropshire Lad with a word left out after 'or'; the missing word fills the gap

explanation.surface: Lines of Housman about carrying beer home from Ludlow, with a gap.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem runs 'And carried half-way home, or near, / Pints and quarts of Ludlow beer': the printed clue drops the word to be supplied.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in Housman's line means close to, almost all the way.

clue.text: Tango air composed for merchant's friend

indicators.note: a piece of music composed puts notes into a new arrangement, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dance tune is written for a businessman's companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composed' rearranges TANGOAIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Gratiano is a friend of Antonio, the title merchant in The Merchant of Venice.

clue.text: Prop object for I supplied by Kingsley Amis?

definitions.text: Prop object for I supplied by Kingsley Amis?

parts.words: Prop object for I supplied by Kingsley Amis?
parts.note: read as a riddle: what belongs to a man called by a certain name, the title of an Amis novel

explanation.surface: Asking what stage property a novelist provided for a performer.
explanation.walkthrough: Amis's 1978 novel is named for its hero Jake's sexual problem; 'object for I' hints at a possessive, what belongs to a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Jake's Thing is a comic novel by Kingsley Amis, its title a possessive naming an object.

clue.text: She advised Roman king — part of a privilege Rialto dwellers demand

indicators.note: only a portion of the words that follow is wanted, the letters running across privilege and Rialto

explanation.surface: Venetians who live near the Rialto bridge insist on their special rights.
explanation.walkthrough: The run is in 'privilEGE RIAlto'.
explanation.definitionFit: Egeria was the nymph who counselled Numa Pompilius, second king of Rome.

clue.text: Well protected but poor claim to youth

indicators.note: a poor claim is a badly made one, so its letters are put in a new order

parts.note: a lad is a youth

explanation.surface: A young man's case is weak though he is well defended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor' rearranges CLAIM to MAILC, then LAD follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Clad in mail, chain armour, a fighter is well protected.

clue.text: Frail vessel of Monsarrat seen in unkind element

definitions.text: Frail vessel of Monsarrat seen in unkind element

parts.words: Frail vessel of Monsarrat seen in unkind element
parts.note: the unkind element is The Cruel Sea, Monsarrat's novel, whose little warship Compass Rose is this class of escort

explanation.surface: A small boat from a war novel tossed on a hostile ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: Nicholas Monsarrat's The Cruel Sea follows a small escort ship in the Atlantic, and he also wrote H.M. Corvette.
explanation.definitionFit: A small, lightly built warship used as a convoy escort in the Second World War.

clue.text: Fleming's Napoleon of anti-crime

parts.note: Moriarty is the Napoleon of crime; on the other side is a spy called Napoleon whom Ian Fleming helped create

explanation.surface: An Ian Fleming crime-fighter likened to a great general.
explanation.walkthrough: Ian Fleming contributed the name of Napoleon Solo, the agent of The Man from U.N.C.L.E.; 'Napoleon of crime' is Holmes's phrase for Moriarty.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon Solo is the secret agent of The Man from U.N.C.L.E., a character Ian Fleming named.

clue.text: Underfed actor began with top billing

explanation.surface: A hungry performer is suddenly given star billing.
explanation.walkthrough: Robin Starveling is the tailor who acts Moonshine in A Midsummer Night's Dream; his name begins with STAR, top billing.
explanation.definitionFit: A starveling is a thin, half-starved creature; Robin Starveling is one of the amateur players in A Midsummer Night's Dream.

clue.text: Admittedly rather nasty Shaw plays

explanation.surface: A reviewer grudgingly finds some of Shaw's dramas rather horrid.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw grouped his early dramas as Plays Pleasant and Plays Unpleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: Disagreeable means rather nasty; Shaw titled a volume of three early dramas Plays Unpleasant.

clue.text: Antony's schoolmaster, and "a poor pinion of his wing "

explanation.surface: A quotation sums up a tutor as a weak feather of his master's wing.
explanation.walkthrough: In Antony and Cleopatra Antony sends his schoolmaster as ambassador to Caesar, and Dolabella calls him 'so poor a pinion of his wing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Euphronius is the schoolmaster Antony sends as envoy, scorned as a poor feather of his wing.

clue.text: A name for Marquis's alley-cat's friend suggests total disorder

parts.note: in Don Marquis's archy and mehitabel, archy the cockroach is friend of mehitabel the alley cat

explanation.surface: A cat's companion's name hints at chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: Don Marquis's archy is a cockroach who types columns, friend of mehitabel the alley cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Anarchy is lawlessness, the absence of all order.

clue.text: A merry wife to be, with "seven hundred pounds and possibilities

definitions.text: A merry wife to be, with "seven hundred pounds and possibilities

parts.words: A merry wife to be, with "seven hundred pounds and possibilities
parts.note: an unmarried girl in The Merry Wives of Windsor, whose dowry Sir Hugh Evans praises in these words

explanation.surface: A bride-to-be brings a handsome dowry and good prospects.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Merry Wives of Windsor Evans says of the Pages' daughter that 'seven hundred pounds and possibilities is goot gifts'.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Page is the daughter courted by three suitors in The Merry Wives of Windsor.

clue.text: Pigeon I cooked for eventual conquerors of Thebes

indicators.note: something cooked is altered, so these letters are made into a new order

explanation.surface: A bird is prepared for victorious warriors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooked' rearranges PIGEONI.
explanation.definitionFit: The Epigoni, sons of the Seven against Thebes, took the city their fathers failed to capture.

clue.text: Wilt thou yet take all, ——' ? but these thou shalt not take " (Swinburne)

definitions.text: Wilt thou yet take all, ——' ? but these thou shalt not take " (Swinburne)

parts.words: Wilt thou yet take all, ——' ? but these thou shalt not take " (Swinburne)
parts.note: a line of Swinburne's Hymn to Proserpine with the person addressed left as a dash to be filled

explanation.surface: A pagan poet defies the new faith in a famous line.
explanation.walkthrough: Swinburne's Hymn to Proserpine addresses Christ by the name of his homeland, Galilee.
explanation.definitionFit: Christ is called the man from Galilee, the person Swinburne's pagan speaker addresses.

clue.text: Tay hulk completely rebuilt for geographer

indicators.note: a hulk rebuilt from scratch has its parts reassembled, so these letters take a new order

explanation.surface: A wreck on the river Tay is reconstructed for a map-maker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'completely rebuilt' rearranges TAYHULK.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Hakluyt was the Elizabethan writer who compiled accounts of English voyages and discoveries.

clue.text: Bunyan market put to novel use

definitions.text: Bunyan market put to novel use

parts.words: Bunyan market put to novel use
parts.note: a fair in The Pilgrim's Progress whose name Thackeray borrowed as a book title

explanation.surface: A market from an allegory is turned to a fresh purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' is the pun: the name was reused for a novel, Thackeray's of 1848.
explanation.definitionFit: Vanity Fair is the town fair in Bunyan's allegory and the title of Thackeray's novel.

clue.text: Should his masterwork be in the Metropolitan Museum of Art?

definitions.text: Should his masterwork be in the Metropolitan Museum of Art?

parts.words: Should his masterwork be in the Metropolitan Museum of Art?
parts.note: a film director whose masterpiece is Metropolis, as if it belonged in a New York gallery named for its city

explanation.surface: Asking whether an artist's best piece belongs in a New York museum.
explanation.walkthrough: Fritz Lang's greatest film is Metropolis, hinted at by 'Metropolitan'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fritz Lang was the German film director of Metropolis (1927).

clue.text: Dramatic sound effects, usually off

parts.note: a stage direction for sounds made behind the scenes, also the title of Frayn's farce

explanation.surface: A theatre's sound effects are often wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noises off' is a stage direction for sounds offstage; 'off' here means offstage, not faulty.
explanation.definitionFit: Sounds made in a theatre to suggest happenings out of sight.

clue.text: "You all did see that on the —— I thrice presented him a kingly crown " (Julius Caesar)

definitions.text: "You all did see that on the —— I thrice presented him a kingly crown " (Julius Caesar)

parts.words: "You all did see that on the —— I thrice presented him a kingly crown " (Julius Caesar)
parts.note: Mark Antony's funeral speech with the name of the festival left as a dash

explanation.surface: Antony reminds the crowd that he offered Caesar a crown three times.
explanation.walkthrough: Antony offered Caesar the crown at the feast of the Lupercalia.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lupercal is the Roman festival, held in February, at which Antony offered Caesar the crown.

clue.text: Turncoat Roman censor

indicators.note: turning a word over rearranges it, so the letters of coat are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A Roman magistrate is a traitor who switched sides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turncoat' looks like one word for a traitor, but 'Turn' rearranges COAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Cato the Elder held the office of censor in Rome in 184 BC and was famed for its severity.

clue.text: J.B. S. Haldane suspected that it was queerer than we suppose, or can suppose

definitions.text: J.B. S. Haldane suspected that it was queerer than we suppose, or can suppose

parts.words: J.B. S. Haldane suspected that it was queerer than we suppose, or can suppose
parts.note: the scientist's famous remark about everything that exists, with that subject replaced by 'it'

explanation.surface: A biologist's remark that reality is stranger than we can imagine.
explanation.walkthrough: Haldane wrote in Possible Worlds: 'the universe is not only queerer than we suppose, but queerer than we can suppose.'
explanation.definitionFit: The cosmos, all of existence, was what Haldane thought stranger than imaginable.

clue.text: Frank friend of Merry and Wharton

definitions.text: Frank friend of Merry and Wharton

parts.words: Frank friend of Merry and Wharton
parts.note: Frank is a first name here, a schoolboy pal of Frank Richards's heroes Tom Merry and Harry Wharton

explanation.surface: A candid companion of two cheerful people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like an adjective, candid; it is a first name, Frank Nugent of the Famous Five of Greyfriars in Frank Richards's school stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Nugent is Harry Wharton's chum at Greyfriars, a fictional English boarding school.

clue.text: The quality of being unlike author of Porterhouse Blue, say?

definitions.text: The quality of being unlike author of Porterhouse Blue, say?

parts.words: The quality of being unlike author of Porterhouse Blue, say?
parts.note: Tom Sharpe wrote the comic novel, so being unlike him is being the opposite of sharp

explanation.surface: Asking what it means to differ from a comic novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Porterhouse Blue is by Tom Sharpe; the opposite of sharp is blunt or dull-witted.
explanation.definitionFit: Dullness of mind, slowness to understand, is the opposite of being sharp.
